Lizzie was still going, though the roughness of the ground had forced her to slow from a gallop to a canter.
That meant I had a chance to catch her. I surged forward.
Blantyre had let me choose my own way while we were on the road, but now he took over again.
With a light hand and a quick eye, he guided me expertly over the tricky ground.
I barely had to slow down. We started to gain on Lizzie.
About halfway across the open area was a wide ditch.
I thought it might make Lizzie stop at last.
Instead she leaped awkwardly across, stumbling on the rough ground on the far side.
Lady Anne was flung to the ground and lay still.
Blantyre groaned. "Now, Black Auster, do your best!" he urged me.
I cleared the ditch with a strong leap, landing safely.
Blantyre pulled me to a stop and leaped down.
He ran to Lady Anne's side while I stood there, my sides heaving after the long gallop.
Two men had been trimming weeds nearby.
One was already chasing Lizzie, who had slowed down after losing her rider.
The other ran toward us.
"Oh no!" he said when he saw Lady Anne lying there still and pale.
"How can I help?"
"Can you ride?" Blantyre asked.
"Not very well," the man said. "But I'll give it a try for Lady Anne's sake.
She's always been so kind to my family."
"Don't worry, this horse will take care of you," Blantyre said, gesturing to me.
"Ride quickly to the doctor's house, then go to Earlshall and let them know what's happened."
The man agreed and mounted.
He wasn't a very good rider, but I didn't mind.
We hurried to the doctor's house, and then back to Earlshall Park.
A groom returned me to the stable while another quickly saddled Ginger for Lady Anne's brother and the others prepared the carriage.
It seemed to take a long time before anyone returned.
At last Ginger arrived back at the stable.
"We galloped almost all the way there," she told me.
"Lady Anne still wasn't moving.
But the doctor was tending to her, and I heard him say she wasn't dead.
Later I heard someone else say that she was lucky she hadn't broken any bones.
So I expect she'll be all right."
The next day Blantyre came to see me.
"You're the finest horse I know, Black Auster," he said as he patted me fondly.
"You seemed to understand the danger as well as I did.
Thanks to your speed and heart, Anne will be fine in a week or two.
And from now on, I'm sure she won't ever want to ride any other horse but you."
Blantyre stayed at Earlshall until Lady Anne recovered from her fall.
Then he returned home.
The head groom, Reuben Smith, drove him to the train since Mr. York was still in London with the earl.
The cart needed some repairs, so Reuben had decided to leave it in town.
He'd brought along a saddle to ride me home.
First he left me at the hotel stable to eat and rest.
The grooms had me ready to leave again at four o'clock.
But Reuben wasn't ready yet. He was having a fine time drinking at the pub.
He didn't show up until almost nine o'clock.
As soon as he climbed into the saddle, I could feel that something wasn't right.
Reuben was normally an excellent rider with a light hand.
Now he swayed back and forth and yanked at the reins.
As we left town, he kicked me into a gallop.
I obeyed, even though I could feel one of my shoes coming loose and it was a little uncomfortable.
"Faster, you!" he shouted, smacking me with his whip. "Faster!"
I didn't understand. I was already going as fast as I could!
My muscles strained, and my shoe loosened more with every stride.
It was a dark night, and I could hardly see where I was going.
That made it impossible to avoid uneven or rocky spots on the road.
We reached a place where the road workers had laid some new stone.
That was when my loose shoe finally came off.
Galloping over the stones on my tender foot was very painful.
I started to slow down, but Reuben struck me again with the whip, so I kept going.
My hoof started to crack as the stones dug into my foot.
No horse could keep going forever under such conditions! But I did my best.
Finally my bare foot hit a slippery patch of gravel.
I stumbled and lurched forward, landing hard on both knees.
Reuben was flung out of the saddle and hit the ground.
I climbed to my feet and limped off to a softer spot.
My knees hurt, my foot was sore, and I was exhausted.
I waited for Reuben to get up, but after a few groans, he lay silent and still.
And so I waited.
The moon rose, and I could see the empty road stretching away in both directions.
Hours passed before I heard a cart approaching.
As it came nearer, I thought I recognized the sound of Ginger's step.
Sure enough she soon came into view pulling two men in a small cart.
The men soon spotted me—and Reuben.
It turned out that Reuben had been killed in the fall.
I wasn't blamed for the accident, as it was easy enough for everyone to figure out what had happened.
One of the men led me carefully back to Earlshall Park, where the grooms tended to my injured knees and wrapped my sore foot.
The foot healed quickly. My knees were another story.
"I don't think the joint is injured," the veterinarian told the grooms.
"This horse should be able to return to full work after a while.
But he'll always have ugly scars on his knees."
"That's too bad," one of the grooms said. "The lady won't like that."
It took a long time for my knees to heal, with lots of painful treatments.
After some time in my stall, the grooms put me out into a small pasture.
I spent a month or so grazing and resting out there.
It was nice, although I was a little lonely.
One day I heard the gate open.
When I looked over, I saw a groom releasing Ginger into the field!
I trotted over to her with a joyful whinny. She was glad to see me too.
But her reason for being there was not a happy one.
She told me the earl's son had been riding her too hard lately.
During a hunt, he'd pressed her so much that she'd ended up with a strained back and breathing problems.
"We are not quite the horses we once were, are we?" she said sadly.
Still we were happy to be together again.
We enjoyed the next few weeks until the earl finally returned from London.
He and York came to see us. The earl frowned as he looked us over.
"What a waste of good horses!" he told York.
"I feel terrible, especially since I told my friend that these two would have a good home here."
"Ginger, the mare, might come around after a rest," York said.
The earl nodded. "We'll give her a chance," he said.
"But I can't have a horse with those knees in my stables.
The black one will have to be sold."
The earl sold me to a man who owned something called a livery stable.
My new home was far away, which meant I had to travel there by train.
That was a frightening day.
I was used to seeing trains, of course, and never got scared when one rushed past.
But climbing onto one and feeling it roar and tremble all around me was a different matter.
For the first few minutes, I trembled as much as the train did.
After a while, though, I realized there was nothing to fear.
I rode the rest of the way quietly. But I was very glad to get off!
At the end of my journey, I was taken to the livery stable.
It wasn't as airy and pleasant as my previous homes, but it wasn't too bad.
The owner and his grooms were kind and experienced.
My new master took a close look at my scarred knees but didn't seem to mind what he saw.
I soon found out what being a livery horse meant.
The master owned lots of horses and many carriages and carts of all different types.
He hired them out to people who didn't have their own.
The first few times I was hired, my master or one of his men drove me.
That wasn't too bad. In fact, it wasn't much different from what I was used to.
Once the master saw how steady and reliable I was, he started hiring me out to people who preferred to drive themselves.
Now that was something different!
Until then I'd only been driven by good drivers.
Even when James was learning, he'd always had John there to help him.
Many of the people who hired me now were not good drivers.
Some liked to keep a very tight hold on the reins at all times.
They never relaxed their pull or allowed me a chance to relax.
Other drivers were just the opposite.
They let the reins lie loose on my back, hardly touching them at all.
That meant they had no control if I should suddenly rear or stumble.
I wasn't the type of horse to do that, so I had little objection to this type of driver.
Still I sometimes missed the steadying hand of my driver, especially while going downhill.
Besides, the loose-rein drivers were often careless about everything.
I once went a good distance with a stone in my foot before a passing farmer noticed and stopped to help me.
My own driver never even realized anything was wrong!
Then there were the customers who cared about nothing but speed.
They seemed to think we horses were just like trains that could go as far and as fast as they pleased.
This type of driving wore me out quicker than any other.
So my work at the livery stable differed from day to day.
Sometimes it was pleasant, and other times it was not.
I got to know the other horses there, especially a mare named Peggy.
Peggy was often paired with me when someone wanted to hire a team.
She was a pretty horse with a sweet temper.
The first time we went out together, I noticed she had an odd walk.
It was neither trot nor canter, but a combination of the two.
Every few strides she would add a little jump forward.
It was very confusing since I had to match my stride to hers.
I finally asked her what made her go in such an odd way.
"I know my gaits are bad," she said, seeming troubled.
"But it's not really my fault. It's because my legs are short.
That means my stride is short, and I have trouble keeping up with longer-legged horses like you!"
Luckily for Peggy, two women liked her so much that they decided to buy her.
After that I saw Peggy several times out in the street.
She was always pulling her mistresses at a good, steady pace and looking very happy.
I shouldn't make it sound as if I had nothing but poor drivers at the livery stable.
Sometimes I was hired by good horsemen.
One such gentleman liked me so much that he wanted to see what I would be like to ride as well.
After riding me several times, he asked my master if he would be willing to sell me.
"My friend is looking for a good, safe horse," the man said.
"I think this fellow would be perfect."
"This horse is one of the most reliable in my stable."
My master stroked his chin.
"But I suppose I'd be willing to part with him for the right price."
A deal was struck, and it was settled. I'd been sold again.
My new owner was named Mr. Barry.
His doctor had advised him to get more exercise, so he'd decided to try riding.
Mr. Barry was a kind man who wanted to do what was best for me, but he didn't know much about horses.
He rented a stall at a stable near his home and hired a groom to take care of me.
The groom's name was Filcher. He was only a part-time groom.
The rest of the time, he and his wife grew fruits and vegetables and raised poultry and rabbits to sell.
At first I liked Filcher well enough.
He kept my stall clean, groomed me thoroughly, and handled me gently.
But after a while, I noticed my grain meals getting smaller and smaller.
That was strange, because Mr. Barry had ordered lots of good food for me.
The grain shouldn't have run out already!
Filcher always arrived at my stall very early. His little son usually came too.
The boy always had a covered basket with him, which he took into the feed room.
After a few minutes, he'd come out again, call good-bye to his father, and scurry off.
I still had hay to eat, but I missed the grain.
It gave me the energy I needed for my work.
One day Mr. Barry rode me to visit a farmer friend of his.
This farmer had a keen eye for horses.
"Your horse doesn't look as good as when you first brought him, Barry," he said.
"Has he been healthy?"
"I think so." Mr. Barry shrugged.
"I've noticed he isn't as lively as he used to be.
My groom told me horses are always dull and weak in the autumn."
"Nonsense!" the farmer exclaimed.
"With your light work he shouldn't have any trouble at any time of the year.
What do you feed him?"
Mr. Barry told him. The farmer felt me all over.
"I don't know who's eating your grain, Barry, but it isn't your horse," he declared.
"You'd better look into it!"
A few mornings later, Filcher and his son arrived at the stable as usual.
The little boy went into the feed room with his basket.
"A-ha!" a voice cried out.
A police officer marched out of the feed room dragging the boy by the arm.
There was a lot of shouting and some crying, and in the end the truth came out.
Filcher had been sending his son to steal my grain!
They sneaked it home in the basket to feed their rabbits.
Mr. Barry was suspicious after talking with his friend, and had asked the police to look into it.
When he found out what had happened, he fired Filcher immediately.
A few days later, my new groom arrived.
He was a tall, good-looking young man named Alfred Smirk.
Mr. Smirk considered himself very handsome.
He spent lots of time on his hair and clothing and always looked his best.
He liked to make me look my best too.
My mane and tail were always neat and glossy, and my hooves were painted with oil.
That was almost all he did for me though.
Smirk was one of the laziest men I'd ever seen.
He rarely bothered to check my feet or shoes or groom me thoroughly.
He did a sloppy job of cleaning my stall, and it soon began to stink.
"Alfred, the stable smells a bit," Mr. Barry said one day.
"Do you think you should scrub out the stall?"
"Well, sir," Smirk said in his polite and charming way, "I can if you like, but it's dangerous to use water in a horse's stall.
It might cause him to catch a cold."
"Oh!" Mr. Barry said. "Perhaps you'd better not then.
But something should be done about the smell.
Perhaps someone should check the drains."
"Good idea, sir," Smirk agreed.
A man came to check my stall.
He found nothing wrong, and the smell went on as always.
The constant dampness began to make my hooves unhealthy and tender.
Eventually my feet got so bad that I couldn't walk over stones without stumbling.
My master became worried and took me to the farrier.
The farrier took one look at my feet and shook his head.
"Your horse has a disease that is caused by standing in wet, dirty stalls.
I'm surprised your groom didn't notice it before it got this bad!"
Mr. Barry was surprised too—and angry.
He directed the farrier to tend to my feet until I was better and fired Smirk immediately.
But this time he had no intention of finding a new groom.
"Having a horse of my own is too much trouble," he told the farrier.
"I'm going to sell this fellow and hire a horse when I need one."
There was a public horse sale near where Mr. Barry had kept me.
People came from all around to sell their horses.
I'd never seen so many horses in one place!
There were young horses that had never left the farm, and ponies that reminded me of Merrylegs.
I saw hundreds of cart horses and riding horses.
Some of the horses were quite fancy.
Others, like me, were solid, respectable animals who had some scars but were still suitable for work.
At the back were the sad cases—the very old, the broken down, the terribly thin.
Only a few people wandered among those hopeless creatures.
But the rest of the place was busy, with plenty of customers looking over the horses.
There was bargaining going on everywhere.
From what I heard and saw, most of it was based on lies and exaggeration.
Mr. Barry had sent me to the sale with a horse trader who promised to sell me for a good price.
I was tied beside a few other strong, useful-looking horses, and lots of people stopped to look at us.
Well-dressed gentlemen always turned away from me as soon as they saw my scarred knees.
But others seemed willing to overlook that.
Most of the shoppers went through the same type of routine.
First, they pulled open my mouth and examined my teeth to see my age.
Then, they looked at my eyes, and felt up and down my legs and body.
Finally, they had the seller trot me around.
Even though the shoppers almost all did the same things, it was amazing how different it could feel, depending on the person.
Some did everything in a rough, impatient way.
They jerked my mouth open and handled my legs as if my legs were made of wood.
Others were gentle, patting me as they went about their examination.
One man seemed kinder than all the rest.
I thought that if he bought me, I might be happy.
He was a small man, but agile and quick.
I could tell right away that he was good with horses.
He spoke gently, and his gray eyes had a cheerful look.
Even the scent of him was pleasing—like fresh hay.
When he finished looking me over, he gave me a pat.
"There's a good boy," he said. Then he turned to the dealer.
"I'll give you 23 pounds for him."
"Sorry, my friend," the dealer said. "This horse is worth at least thirty."
The gray-eyed man shrugged and moved on.
I watched him go, wishing he would come back.
Instead a hard-faced man with a loud voice came to look at me.
His hands were rough and careless as he checked me over.
I was relieved when he left without saying a word to the dealer.
I definitely didn't want to go home with a man like that!
A few more shoppers came by, but none showed much interest in me.
Then the hard-faced man returned.
"23 pounds for the black horse," he told the dealer. "It's a fair price."
The dealer hesitated.
We'd been there for a while, and I guess he thought he might not get the price he wanted for me.
Before he could speak, the kind, gray-eyed man came toward me again.
I couldn't help reaching out my head toward him, and he stroked my face.
"Hello, old boy," he told me. "Perhaps we're meant to be together after all."
He looked at the dealer. "I'll give you 24."
The hard-faced man shook his head and walked away. The dealer smiled.
"Say 25, and he's yours," he said.
"Twenty-four ten, and not a penny more," the gray-eyed man replied.
"Done!" said the dealer. "And he's a bargain at that price, my friend.
There's a lot of quality in this horse.
If you want him for cab work, you won't be disappointed."
The gray-eyed man paid for me, then took me by the halter and led me away from the sale.
We walked to a nearby inn, where he gave me some food and water.
A half hour later, my new owner saddled me, and we were on our way.
We rode down pleasant country lanes and wider roads.
The farther we went, the more crowded the roads became.
Finally we reached a highway and rode into a bustling place.
I'd never seen anything like it!
There were streets to the left, streets to the right, and streets crossing one another for mile upon mile.
Horses, carriages, and people were everywhere.
There were new sights, new sounds, and new smells.
It was so overwhelming that I was glad my new owner was there in the saddle to guide me through it all.
We had arrived in the big city called London.
My new owner's name was Jerry Barker.
He rode me to a narrow street lined with shabby-looking houses on one side and modest stables on the other.
Stopping in front of one house, he whistled.
The door flew open, and Jerry's family rushed out.
His wife was a plump, pretty woman known as Polly.
Jerry also had a twelve-year-old son, Harry, and an eight-year-old daughter, Dolly.
All three of them were just as cheerful and kind as Jerry himself.
They were the most happy, loving family I'd ever seen.
Soon all four of them were standing around me in a small but clean stable.
"Is he gentle, Father?" Dolly asked.
"Yes, Dolly," Jerry told her. "He's as gentle as a kitten. Come and pat him."
While the little girl patted me, her mother hurried inside to make me a bran mash.
Jerry and his son lined my stall with soft straw, and soon I was comfortable and happy.
The family decided to call me Jack, after a fine old horse they'd once had.
There was one other horse in the stable.
He was a gray, large-boned animal who had a proud and handsome look, despite his great age.
His name was Captain, and he'd once been a war horse in the Crimean War.
As we got to know each other, Captain told me many stories about those days.
Some were fine tales about marching in formation with the other horses.
Others were terrible stories about seeing awful things during the fighting.
I soon learned that Jerry was a cab driver.
People hired him to drive them places in his cab, which was a boxy black carriage.
On my first day, Jerry took Captain out with the cab in the morning.
When they returned in the afternoon, it was my turn.
Jerry took his time putting on my harness, making sure it fit me as well as possible.
Even John Manly from Birtwick Park couldn't have been more careful!
Best of all, there was no checkrein and no harsh bit, so I was quite comfortable.
When I was hitched to the cab, Jerry drove me down the narrow street and out into a wider one.
We stopped at the cab stand, which was where all the taxicabs waited for customers on the street.
The block was lined with shops on one side and an old church and churchyard on the other.
There were several cabs lined up there already when we arrived, and all the drivers called or waved to Jerry.
A couple of the men came over to look at me.
"He's very nice-looking," one of them said.
"He's too nice-looking," another added.
"There must be something wrong with him. You'll find out one of these days."
"Perhaps," Jerry said with a chuckle.
"But until then, I won't waste time worrying about it."
Another man was approaching.
He had a broad, jolly face and a huge gray cape with a matching hat.
The other men made way for him as he came toward me.
I would later learn that he was known as the Governor.
He'd been working at the cab stand for longer than anyone else, and the others all respected his opinions a great deal.
The Governor looked me over carefully.
"He's the right type of horse for you, Jerry," he declared at last.
"I don't care what you paid for him. He'll be worth it."
And so my life as a London cab horse began.
For the first week, I found it difficult to get used to my new job.
The noise, the crowds, and the hurry made me feel anxious most of the time.
But I soon found that I could trust Jerry to help me through it.
He was as good a driver as I'd ever known, and paid as much attention to his horses' comfort as he did to his own.
He soon found out that I was always willing to work and do my best.
After that he never used the whip on me except to draw it gently across my back to ask me to move on.
Before long my master and I understood each other as well as horse and man can.
Jerry was good to us in the stable too.
Captain and I always had enough food and water.
Jerry took off our halters at night so we could move around our stalls at will.
But there was one thing Jerry did for us that was even better than the rest.
He always gave us Sundays off.
We worked so hard during the week that I was always glad when Sunday came.
Jerry believed a day off was necessary for man and animal, and he always lived as he believed.
As I've said, Jerry Barker believed in having Sundays off.
Spending time with his family was worth more to him than any money he might earn.
One day he was hitching me to the cab when a gentleman walked into the stable yard.
I recognized the man. We often carried him and his wife around town.
"Good morning, Mr. Briggs," Jerry said politely.
"Good morning," the gentleman replied.
"I came to offer you a business arrangement.
Mrs. Briggs and I have decided to try a new church, and it's too far to walk.
We'd like to have you drive us there each Sunday morning."
"Thank you, sir," Jerry said. "But I'm afraid I can't. I never work on Sundays."
"I understand, but of course we'd pay extra for your trouble," Mr. Briggs said.
"It would only be a short trip."
Jerry shook his head. "I'm sorry, sir.
I used to work seven days a week, and it was miserable.
Year in and year out, never a day's rest for me or the horses.
I didn't get to spend any time with my wife and children.
For the past five years I've made it a rule not to work on Sundays, and we're all happier than we've ever been."
"I see." Mr. Briggs frowned. "I suppose I'll have to find another cab."
He walked away, and Jerry gave me a pat.
"I'm afraid I've disappointed him, Jack," he said.
"But we can't give up our Sundays."
When Polly came outside, he told her what had happened.
"It was difficult to say no," Jerry said.
"Mrs. Briggs is one of my best customers.
She often goes shopping or visiting for hours at a time, and always pays the whole fare without arguing.
She's never in a hurry, and driving her around is easy work for the horses.
We might lose her as a customer because of this. What do you think, Polly?"
"I think you did the right thing," Polly said.
"I remember how things were when you worked all the time.
I wouldn't go back to those days even if you earned twice what you do now!"
For three weeks after that, we saw no sign of Mrs. Briggs.
I could tell Jerry missed both her company and her fares.
One evening Polly announced that a servant had come that day to ask Jerry to pick up Mrs. Briggs the next morning.
"I said you would, of course," Polly said.
"But I also said I was surprised, since we thought Mrs. Briggs had hired someone else."
"What did the servant say?" Jerry asked.
"He said Mr. Briggs was annoyed that you wouldn't work on Sundays, so he'd been trying other cabs," Polly reported.
"But Mrs. Briggs wasn't happy with any of them.
Some drove too fast, some too slow, and none were as nice and clean as yours.
So she insisted they hire you again!"
Jerry was glad to have his favorite customer back.
He was just as glad he'd stood by his decision not to work on Sundays.
But one day soon after that, he made an exception to his Sunday rule.
A neighbor needed a ride out into the country to visit her dying mother, and he agreed to take her.
"It's the right thing to do," Polly agreed when he told her.
"Poor Dinah has no other option.
And we should always try to treat others as we'd like to be treated.
I would certainly appreciate a ride to visit my own mother if I needed it."
I was chosen for the journey, and we set out.
I was tired from the work week, but Jerry had borrowed a lighter cart for the trip.
After the heavy four-wheeled cab, it felt easy to pull.
It was a fine May day, and it was nice to leave the city behind and breathe the fresh country air.
Dinah's family lived in a small farmhouse.
Two cows were grazing peacefully in the grassy field behind it.
"You can tie your horse in the cowshed while you wait," a young man said.
"I wish we had a better stable to offer you."
"If your cows wouldn't mind, I'm sure there's nothing my horse would like better than an hour or two out in the grass," Jerry said.
The young man agreed gladly.
Jerry led me into the field, removed my harness, and set me free.
I could hardly believe my good fortune!
At first I wasn't sure what to do. Should I graze? Roll in the soft grass?
Lie down to rest? Or gallop across the field out of sheer freedom?
I did all those things.
Jerry smiled as he watched me, and I knew he was glad we had come—even on a Sunday.
That winter was especially cold and wet.
There was snow, sleet, or rain almost every day for weeks, and the wind made things even worse.
It was miserable standing at the cab stand for hours at a time.
At least Captain and I only had to put up with it for half a day each.
Poor Jerry was out there all day, huddled in his cab trying to keep warm.
To help him through it, Polly often sent Dolly to the cab stand with hot food.
One such cold, rainy day, Jerry had barely started eating when a gentleman came hurrying toward us, raising his umbrella to signal that he wanted to hire the cab.
When Jerry saw him, he immediately handed his bowl back to Dolly, who was still standing there keeping him company.
"No, no!" the gentleman cried when he saw what Jerry was doing.
"Finish your soup, my friend.
I don't have much time to spare, but I can wait until you're done and your little girl is safely off toward home."
With that, he climbed into the cab and sat down to wait.
Jerry thanked him, and then turned to Dolly.
"That's a true gentleman, Dolly," he told her quietly.
"He isn't too wrapped up in his own concerns to spare a thought for a poor cabman and his girl!"
He quickly finished his soup, and sent Dolly home.
We drove the gentleman to his destination, and I suppose he was pleased with our work because after that he hired us on a regular basis.
The gentleman's name was Mr. Wright.
I think he was fond of horses, because he often stopped to pat me and give me a kind word.
It's a rare thing indeed for customers to pay any attention to a cab horse.
With few exceptions, most people would be just as likely to pat the engine of a train!
One day Mr. Wright and a gentleman friend of his hired our cab to take them to do some shopping.
The second gentleman went into a store while Mr. Wright stood and waited outside.
I saw Mr. Wright watching a pair of fine-looking horses that were standing across the street in front of a wine seller's cart.
Their driver was nowhere in sight, and after a few minutes the horses grew restless.
They weren't tied, so they started forward on their own.
They'd only gone a few steps down the street when a man emerged from the nearest shop.
He raced after the cart, shouting angrily.
When he caught up to the horses, he immediately started whipping both of them as hard as he could.
He even struck them on their heads. It was terrible to watch!
Mr. Wright saw it all. He crossed the street and hurried toward the wine cart.
"Stop that right now!" he called to the driver in a stern voice.
"Otherwise I'll have you arrested for leaving your horses unattended and for cruel conduct!"
The man spun around, looking surprised.
He frowned and cursed at Mr. Wright, but at least he stopped whipping the horses.
As the driver jumped into his cart, Mr. Wright pulled out a notebook and wrote down the name and address painted on the cart.
"What are you doing?" the driver demanded.
But Mr. Wright merely smiled and didn't answer.
He returned to the cab just as his friend came out of the shop.
When the friend heard what had been going on, he laughed.
"Don't you have enough business of your own to look after, Wright, without worrying about other people's horses and servants?" he said.
Mr. Wright frowned and was silent for a moment.
"Do you know why this world is as bad as it is?" he said at last in a serious tone.
"No," his friend said. "Why?"
"It's because people think only about themselves," Mr. Wright told him.
"They aren't willing to help the oppressed or stand up to wrongdoers.
I can't watch anyone acting in a cruel way without trying to put a stop to it.
If I didn't, I'd consider myself just as guilty as the one committing the wrong."
"I see your point, my friend," the other gentleman said, sounding impressed.
Mr. Wright nodded.
"Many a business owner has thanked me for letting him know his horses were being mistreated.
I'm sure the wine seller will be no exception.
Let's go right now and let him know what I saw."
Jerry had been sitting in the cab listening to all this.
He tipped his cap to Mr. Wright.
"I wish there were more gentlemen like you, sir," he said.
"The city would be better for it."
Winter turned to spring and the weather got much better, though the life of a London cab horse is always hard.
Still I knew I had it better than many. I found out just how much better one day.
Jerry's cab and several others were waiting at the edge of a park.
There was a concert in the park that day.
The cabbies knew that lots of people would be looking for a ride home after the music was over.
While we were standing there, a shabby old cab stopped beside ours.
The horse pulling it was an old, worn-out chestnut mare.
She had a dull coat, and you could count every rib on her thin sides.
Jerry had put out some hay for me to eat while we waited.
The wind blew a few strands over toward the other horse, and she stretched out her long, thin neck to pick it up.
Then she turned and looked around for more with her hopeless eyes.
I thought there was something familiar about her.
Before I could figure it out, she looked at me and cried, "Black Beauty! Is that you?"
It was Ginger! But it was no wonder I hadn't recognized her at first.
She looked like a different horse.
Her beautiful arched neck was now straight and thin.
Her long, delicate legs were swollen from hard work.
And her face, which had once been so full of life and spirit, now showed only suffering.
She coughed, and I could tell her breathing problems were worse than ever.
What had happened to her?
Our drivers were standing together a short distance away, so I moved a step or two closer so Ginger and I could talk.
"They rested me at Earlshall for a year or so," she began.
"By then I had recovered enough to be fit for work again.
The earl's son had lost interest in me, so I was sold to a gentleman in the area."
"Was he a kind master?" I asked.
"He was all right," Ginger replied. "We got along pretty well at first.
But one day he took me for a longer gallop than usual, and my breathing problems returned."
"Oh no!" I murmured.
"The gentleman had me rested and treated again, but then he sold me too," Ginger said.
She went on to describe what had happened next.
She'd changed hands several times, always ending up in a worse situation than before.
Each owner had quickly realized she couldn't work hard without her health problems returning.
"Finally I was sold to a man who keeps a number of cabs and horses.
He leases them out to drivers who can't afford their own," Ginger said.
"When he found out about my breathing problems, he decided to send me out with one of his cheapest cabs.
The driver doesn't care how hard he uses me.
All he cares about is making enough to pay his lease and have some profit left over.
So I work all the time, never even getting a day's rest."
"How terrible!" I said.
"But you used to stand up for yourself when you were mistreated, Ginger."
"I know," she said with a heavy sigh. "But what's the point?
If humans decide to treat us badly, they're going to do it no matter what.
All we can do is bear it as best we can until the end.
I'm glad you seem to have a kind master, Beauty.
As for me, I look forward to the day when all this will end."
I felt very sad, especially when I remembered what a fine horse she'd once been.
I could think of nothing to say that might make things better.
So I put my nose close to hers, trying to comfort her.
"You're the only friend I ever had," she told me.
Just then her driver hurried over and hopped into the cab.
With a yank at the reins, he drove her away, leaving me feeling very troubled.
It was only a week or so later that a cart carrying a dead horse passed by the cab stand.
The horse's head hung lifelessly over the back edge.
It was such a dreadful sight that I couldn't look for long.
I saw enough, however, to know that the horse was a chestnut with a long neck and a white blaze.
I believe it was my friend Ginger lying there in that cart.
I hope it was her anyway. That would mean her suffering is over at last.
We came home one day to find Polly waiting. "Jerry!" she cried.
"One of the candidates was here today.
He wants to hire your cab for the election next week."
"You can tell him to find a different cab," Jerry said.
"I don't want anyone's election posters plastered all over mine."
Election Day was when the humans chose their leaders.
It seemed to make many people act strangely.
Even poor Dolly got teased by some naughty boys who thought her father supported the wrong party.
It was all very perplexing to me.
When Election Day arrived, Jerry and I had all the work we could handle.
Many other cabs had been hired by the candidates and were busy dashing around town encouraging people to vote.
That made the streets even more crowded and hectic than usual.
We saw two people who were trying to cross the street get knocked down by speeding cabs!
We'd just returned to the cab stand when a young woman came toward us.
Her clothes were old and plain, and she was carrying a child in her arms.
The woman's expression was confused and anxious.
The child was crying in a feeble voice.
"Excuse me, sir," the young woman said to Jerry.
"Could you please tell me how to get to St. Thomas' Hospital?
I'm visiting from the country and don't know my way around London.
I certainly didn't expect all this commotion!"
"The election is today," Jerry said.
"If you don't mind my asking, why do you need to find the hospital?"
"It's my son," she said.
"He's four years old, but he can't walk any better than a baby.
He's always in pain.
The doctors said if I can get him to the hospital, they might be able to help him.
So that's where I'm taking him."
"You can't be thinking of walking!" Jerry exclaimed.
"The hospital is three miles away, and that child looks heavy."
"Yes, he is," the woman said with a sad smile.
"But I'm strong, and I've come this far."
"No, the crowds are bad today," Jerry said firmly.
"You and your child could be run over.
Just get in my cab, ma'am, and I'll drive you."
"Thank you, but I couldn't, sir," the woman said.
"I only have enough money to pay my way back home."
Jerry shook his head. "Forget about the money.
I have a wife and children at home, and it would be an honor to help you.
Now climb in, and I'll take you there for free."
"Heaven bless you!" the woman cried, bursting into tears.
As Jerry opened the door to let her into the cab, two well-dressed men rushed over.
They were both wearing election colors.
"Cab!" one of them called.
"Engaged," Jerry said.
The men didn't seem to hear him.
They were already pushing past the woman, and were soon seated in the cab.
"Excuse me, gentlemen," Jerry said.
"I told you, this cab is already engaged by that lady."
One of the men gave the young woman a brief glance.
"I'm sure she can wait," he said. "Our business is very important."
"Besides," added the other man, "we got in first. That means it's our cab."
Jerry shut the door behind them. "All right, gentlemen.
Stay in as long as you like." He turned to the young woman.
"Don't worry," he told her with a smile.
"They'll be gone soon enough."
It took only a few minutes for the men to realize that Jerry didn't intend to drive them anywhere.
They climbed out of the cab and hurried off, calling him all sorts of bad names.
Jerry helped the woman and child into the cab, and then drove them to the hospital.
The woman climbed out with many thanks, which I could see pleased Jerry greatly.
We were about to depart when a well-dressed lady came down the hospital steps, looking for a cab.
As soon as she saw Jerry, she smiled broadly.
"Jeremiah Barker! Is that you?" she exclaimed.
Jerry seemed equally glad to see her.
From listening to their conversation, I discovered that the lady lived on a fine estate in the country.
Polly had worked for her family before marrying Jerry and moving to London.
"How does cab work suit you?" the lady asked Jerry.
"I know your dear wife was anxious about your health last year."
"Yes, ma'am, she was," Jerry replied.
"I had a cough all winter, and the long hours and bad weather can be difficult.
"But I wouldn't know what to do with myself if I didn't have horses to look after."
The lady smiled. "I understand.
Just remember, there's always a need for good grooms and drivers.
If you ever want to give up the cab life, just let me know."
I had become good friends with Jerry's other horse, Captain.
The noble, old war horse was good company, and I never imagined that he would leave us.
And I suppose he wouldn't have, if not for the accident.
I wasn't there, so I only know what I heard.
It seemed that Jerry and Captain had just dropped off a customer when they heard a terrible commotion nearby.
"Clear the way!" someone yelled. "Runaway cart!"
Jerry and Captain turned to see something terrible.
A cart pulled by a team of large, panicky draft horses was out of control and racing toward them!
It all happened so fast that Jerry and Captain couldn't move out of the way in time.
The cart crashed into them, knocking over both cab and horse.
Jerry was thrown free and escaped with only bumps and bruises.
Poor Captain wasn't so lucky.
It was a sad sight to see him limp into the stable, sore and bleeding from numerous cuts and gashes.
Jerry and the vet did all they could for him, and for a while he seemed to be getting better.
But Captain was a very old horse, and Jerry soon realized he would never be fit for cab work again.
"He might recover well enough for you to sell him," the vet said.
"He could bring a few pounds at the horse sale from someone who needs a cart horse."
"Absolutely not!" Jerry said firmly.
"I won't sell a good old friend into hard work and misery.
It's much kinder to put him down here at home.
That way I'll know he won't suffer anymore."
The next day Jerry's son, Harry, took me to the blacksmith for some new shoes.
When I returned, Captain was gone.
I missed the old fellow a lot, and I know Jerry and his family did too.
But the cab had been fixed by then, and there was work to do, so Jerry began the search for a new horse.
He ran into a young man from a nobleman's stables.
That young man told him about a certain horse in his care.
This horse was young and well-bred, but he'd run away with the carriage and caused an accident.
This left him too blemished for a gentleman's stables so the young man had to sell him.
"He's not the typical cab horse," the friend warned Jerry.
"He's young and quite spirited."
"I can deal with high spirits as long as the horse isn't nasty," Jerry said.
"He's not nasty or vicious at all," the young man said.
"In my opinion, the accident wasn't his fault.
It was a cool day, and the horse hadn't had enough exercise that week.
The checkrein was very tight, and the bit rather harsh.
I think the combination made the horse lose his mind."
"That makes sense to me," Jerry said.
"Perhaps all he needs is some fair treatment and an honest day's work to settle him down.
I'll come see him tomorrow."
The next day the horse came home with Jerry. His name was Hotspur.
He was only five years old and very handsome.
I greeted him as he looked around the stable.
He answered politely, but seemed distracted.
"It can't be true!" he said. "Am I really reduced to being a humble cab horse?"
"It's not a bad life," I told him. "Yes, the work can be hard.
But Jerry and his family are the kindest masters you could have."
Hotspur snorted and didn't answer.
He seemed disgusted, and spent most of that first night moving around so restlessly that I couldn't sleep.
But after five or six hours of pulling the cab the following day, he returned to the stable seeming much quieter and more sensible.
Jerry spent a lot of time with him that first week, and before long they understood each other almost as well as Jerry and I did.
"See?" Jerry told his son, Harry, one day.
"With an easy bit in his mouth and plenty of work, our Hotspur will soon be as gentle as a lamb.
That nobleman's loss is our gain.
Now we have a fine, strong young horse with many good years ahead of him."
Even Hotspur himself seemed to agree.
"I suppose I could have ended up in a worse place," he said that evening after we'd finished our grain.
"At least here I don't have to wear that horrible checkrein.
And the bit is much softer than my old one. That makes up for a lot."
I agreed with that, of course.
Before long Hotspur had settled in so well that it was hard to remember what things were like without him.
The holiday season is busy for cab drivers and their horses.
People rush about to parties and balls, and nobody wants to walk in the chilly weather.
Jerry was glad for the extra work, though the cough he'd had last winter returned.
When New Year's Eve arrived, a pair of men hired him to take them to a party.
We dropped them off at a fancy house at nine o'clock.
"Come pick us up at eleven," one of the men directed.
"But it's a card party.
If we're not finished with our game, you might have to wait a few minutes."
Jerry was always punctual. At eleven o'clock we were back in front of the house.
The party was still going on inside.
Fifteen minutes passed, and then thirty.
By the time the clock chimed twelve, the door still hadn't opened.
It was a cold, windy evening.
As we stood waiting, the rain started and quickly turned to sleet.
Jerry covered me with my blanket, but there was no shelter for him.
He walked up and down the block, trying to keep warm, but that made him cough more than ever.
Finally he huddled in the door of his cab.
At twelve thirty he went to the door of the house to ask if his services were still wanted.
"Yes, they'll be out pretty soon," a servant told him.
Another forty-five minutes passed before the party finally ended.
The two gentlemen came out and climbed into the cab without a word of apology.
My legs were numb from standing in the cold, and I was glad to be moving.
We dropped off the men and headed home, where Polly was waiting up for us as usual.
By that time Jerry was coughing so hard he could barely speak.
"Please get Jack something warm," he told his worried wife.
She hurried inside while Jerry took off the harness and groomed me.
Polly soon brought me a warm mash that made me feel as good as new.
Nobody came to the stable until late the next morning.
Finally young Harry showed up.
He fed us, cleaned our stalls, and then left again.
"What's going on?" Hotspur wondered. "It's not Sunday, is it?"
"No," I said. "This is strange."
Harry returned a few hours later. This time his sister was with him.
She was crying.
"Don't worry," Harry told her. "Father will get better."
"But he's so sick!" Dolly cried. "What if he doesn't?"
For two days we didn't see anyone but Harry and sometimes Dolly.
Both children looked worried all the time.
On the third day, Harry was in the stable when there was a tap at the door.
It was the older cab driver known as the Governor.
"I didn't want to bother your parents, my boy," he said to Harry.
"How's your father doing?"
"He's pretty sick," Harry said, his voice shaking a little.
"The doctor says it's bronchitis."
"Oh dear," the Governor said. "That can be very bad indeed!
But if anyone can pull through, it's your father."
The next day the Governor came back.
When he heard that Jerry was still very ill, he offered to take Hotspur out with his own cab.
"Jack will be all right with a week or two of rest," he told Harry.
"You can walk him up and down the street to stretch his legs.
But this young horse is another matter."
"Yes," Harry admitted.
"Hotspur is already getting restless even though I'm giving him less grain."
The Governor offered to take Hotspur out every day and give half of what he earned to Jerry and Polly.
That went on for a week or so.
It worked out well for everyone involved, including the Governor's own horses, who got a little extra rest.
Meanwhile Jerry was finally getting better.
But the doctor told him he should never go back to cab work if he wanted to live to old age.
One afternoon Harry was in the stable when Dolly came rushing in.
"Who lives at Fairstowe?" she asked.
"Mother just got a letter from there, and she looks very excited!"
"Fairstowe? That's the name of the place where Mother worked before she married Father," Harry said.
"Remember? Father said he ran into the lady who lived there last summer."
"I wonder what she's writing about?" Dolly said.
We soon found out. Polly's old mistress had heard about Jerry's illness.
She wanted the whole family to come and live in the cottage on her estate!
Her coachman was retiring soon, and Jerry could take his place.
Hotspur and I were happy for our kind master, of course.
But we were sad too.
Jerry wouldn't be able to take us with him, and so we both had to be sold.
Jerry and his family were very sad about leaving their horses behind.
I was sad too.
I'd never known such a good master since my days at Birtwick Park.
When the Governor heard what was happening, he offered to buy Hotspur.
There were other cab drivers who would have taken me, but Jerry said no.
He thought it was time to find me easier work.
I was sold to a local baker who needed a horse.
Jerry had known him for a long time and thought he'd give me a good home.
In a way he was right. The baker himself was kind and fair.
But he stayed busy in his shop, leaving the management of his delivery carts to his foreman.
The foreman was always in a hurry.
He often added more weight to an already full load.
My driver, Jakes, sometimes protested when the foreman overloaded my cart.
"This horse isn't young," Jakes would say.
"He shouldn't pull so much weight."
"Why make two trips if you can fit everything in one?" the foreman always replied.
"Getting things done faster is better for business."
The heavy loads were bad enough.
To make things worse, all the drivers at this place used a checkrein, and Jakes was no exception.
That made it difficult to pull even a normal load!
By the time I'd been there a few months, I could already feel myself losing strength and spirit.
One day my cart was loaded even more heavily than usual.
Part of our route took us up a very steep hill.
"Go on, Blackie," Jakes called, flicking the whip at me.
I started up the hill, but could only go a short way before I had to stop.
Jakes urged me on, and I took a few more steps before I had to rest again.
Jakes began to lose patience.
"Go on, you lazy fellow!" he called, whipping me a little harder.
Once again I struggled on, pulling the heavy load a few more yards.
When I stopped to catch my breath, I felt the whip cut me again.
I surged forward, but I couldn't move the cart much farther.
The whip came again.
It pained me, but it hurt even more to know that I was being punished while doing my very best.
"Excuse me, sir!" a sweet voice called out just as Jakes raised the whip again.
"Please don't whip your horse anymore.
The road is very steep, and I'm sure he's doing the best he can."
The speaker was a fine-looking lady.
Jakes gave her a respectful nod as he answered.
"If doing his best won't get us where we're going, he'll have to do a little more," he said.
"It looks like a very heavy load," the lady said.
"Yes, it is," Jakes replied. "But that's not my fault.
The foreman insisted on adding more to the cart, and now it's up to me to deliver it."
He raised the whip again. The lady held up a hand.
"Please, sir," she said in an earnest voice.
"At least give the horse a fair chance.
He can't use all his strength with his head held back that way.
If you take off the checkrein, I'm sure he'll do better.
Will you try it, please, as a favor to me?"
Jakes looked surprised, but he tipped his hat.
"Anything to please a lady," he said.
"How far would you like me to loosen it, ma'am?"
"All the way," she told him. "Just give him his head."
Jakes shrugged and came forward.
When he unbuckled the checkrein, I could hardly believe the relief!
I stretched forward immediately, and tossed my head several times to shake the painful stiffness from my neck and shoulders.
"Poor fellow! It looks like you needed that," the lady said, patting me.
Jakes took me by the bridle. "Come on, Blackie. Let's give it another try."
I put down my head and threw my strength against the load.
The cart moved on, and this time I could pull it all the way up the hill.
The lady walked along with us.
When we reached the top, she gave me another pat.
"There, you see?" she told Jakes with a sweet smile.
"I hope you'll consider leaving off the checkrein from now on."
When she left, Jakes shook his head. "That was a real lady," he said to himself.
"She spoke to me as politely as if I were a gentleman rather than a humble cart driver."
After that he loosened the checkrein a little.
Even so, the heavy loads continued to wear me out.
Before long the foreman brought in a younger horse to take my place.
That left me to wonder once again what would become of me.
The baker's foreman sold me to Nicholas Skinner, the owner of a large cab company.
Skinner's company was like the one poor Ginger had worked for in her last days.
He owned many cabs and horses, which he leased out to his drivers.
He was hard on the men, and the men were hard on the horses.
There were no Sundays off and no rest, even in the worst heat of summer.
My driver had a cruel whip with a sharp end that sometimes drew blood.
When I didn't respond fast enough, he whipped me under the belly or on the head.
It was terrible!
I'd always worked willingly for Jerry because he was a kind master.
Now I worked because I had no other choice.
It was a wretched life.
I found myself thinking of poor Ginger and hoping, like her, to drop dead soon and escape my misery.
One day that wish almost came to pass.
It was a very hot day.
My driver and I reached the cab stand at eight in the morning.
We were at work almost immediately, carrying several customers here and there.
The last one needed to go to the train station.
After we dropped him off, we took our place at the end of the line of cabs, waiting for fares.
A large train pulled in, and soon all the other cabs were taken.
Finally it was our turn.
A family of four hurried toward us.
There was a loud-voiced man, his wife, and their young son and daughter.
They had lots of luggage, which the porters started loading onto the cab.
The little girl looked at me.
"Papa, this poor horse looks so weak and worn-out!
Do you think he'll be able to pull us and all of our luggage?"
"Don't worry, miss," my driver said. "He's strong enough."
"He does look tired," a porter said.
"Maybe you should hire a second cab to take part of the load."
Once again my driver insisted that I could do it.
When the little girl tried to protest, her father shushed her.
"Get into the cab, Grace," he said.
"This driver knows his business better than we do.
That's the last I want to hear about it."
The little girl had no choice but to obey.
Soon all the luggage was loaded, and we set out.
I managed fairly well until we reached a hill.
The load seemed to pull at me more than ever.
I struggled on, doing my best as always.
My driver urged me on with his voice and whip.
Suddenly my feet slipped out from under me.
I fell to the ground, landing heavily on my side.
All I could do was lie there, my sides heaving while I struggled to breathe.
Despite my driver's shouts, I couldn't even move.
I thought this was it—now I was going to die.
"That poor horse!" I heard the little girl's voice cry out. "It's our fault."
Other louder voices quickly drowned her out. There was confusion all around me.
Someone came and loosened my bridle and unfastened the harness.
"I think he's dead," someone said.
"No, he's still breathing, see?" someone else said.
I'm not sure how much time passed after that.
Someone poured cold water on my head, and a blanket was laid over my body.
After a while a kind-voiced man came and patted me and urged me to rise.
By then I was able to obey.
It was a struggle, but finally I found myself back on my feet, trembling and weak.
The kind man led me to a stable nearby, and the people there took care of me for the evening.
The next day I was strong enough for the walk back to my owner's stable.
The owner and the vet came to see me.
"There's nothing really wrong with this horse," the vet told Skinner after he examined me.
"He's just been overworked.
If you give him six months off, he should be able to work again."
"I don't have time for that," Skinner said.
"I guess he's no good for anything but dog food."
The vet shook his head. "He's not that far gone.
Rest him and feed him well for ten days.
Then you should be able to get something for him at the next horse sale."
Skinner decided to take the vet's advice.
He ordered his men to take good care of me for the next ten days.
By the day of the horse sale I was feeling as if life might be worth living after all.
So I held up my head and hoped for the best.
The last time I'd been at a horse sale, I'd stood out front with the strong, useful horses.
This time I found myself in the back among the old, broken-down, used-up creatures.
The people who came to look at us weren't much better.
They were mostly poor and hopeless-looking themselves.
Sometimes a shopper from the nicer part of the sale would wander past.
One of these was a gentleman farmer with a kind, ruddy face. A boy was with him.
The gentleman saw me and stopped. I pricked my ears and looked at him.
"Look, Willie," the man said to the boy.
"Now there's a horse that's known better days."
"Do you think he was ever a carriage horse, Grandpa?" the boy asked.
"I wouldn't be surprised," his grandfather replied.
"He might have been anything when he was young.
If you look beyond his poor condition, you can still see his fine breeding."
He gave me a pat on the neck.
I stretched my nose toward him in response, and the boy stroked my face.
"Look how sweet he is!" the boy said.
"Can't you buy him and make him young again, like you did with Ladybird?"
"I can't make all old horses young, Willie," the farmer said.
"Besides, Ladybird wasn't that old. She was just run-down and treated badly."
"How do you know this one's any older, Grandpa?" Willie replied.
"He still has a nice-looking mane and tail, and his eyes aren't sunken in like some old horses.
At least check his teeth to see his age."
The farmer laughed. "You're as horsey as your old grandfather," he teased.
The man from Skinner's stable had been listening to all this.
"Your grandson is right, sir," he spoke up.
"This horse isn't terribly old, just tired out from cab work.
I heard the vet say he'd be good as new with six months' rest.
And you won't find a better-tempered animal anywhere."
The farmer talked with him a little more, then felt my legs and looked into my mouth.
"Thirteen or fourteen, I'd guess," he said. "Could you trot him for us?"
The other man jogged me in a circle.
I arched my thin neck and stretched out my stiff legs as best I could.
"What's the lowest you'll take for him?" the farmer asked.
"Five pounds, sir. That was the lowest price my boss set."
"It's taking a chance," the farmer said with a sigh.
He pulled out some money and handed it to the man.
Young Willie could hardly contain his joy as they led me away.
When they got me home, the farmer told his workers to turn me out in a grassy field to rest.
He also wanted me to have hay and grain every day.
"He'll be your special project, my boy," he told Willie.
"You're in charge of his care from now on."
Willie was proud of his new job and took it very seriously.
He came to see me every day, spending time with me and making sure I had enough to eat.
His name for me was Old Crony.
I spent that winter with complete rest, plenty of food, kind people, and pleasant surroundings.
By spring I was feeling almost young again!
Finally the farmer decided it was time to try me in harness.
He and Willie hooked me to a small carriage and drove me a few miles.
By then my legs were no longer stiff, and I enjoyed the work.
"He's growing young, Willie," the farmer said with a smile.
"We'll give him a little easy work to get him fit again.
By summer he'll be as good as Ladybird.
He's well-trained and has very good gaits."
"I'm so glad you bought him, Grandpa!" the boy said.
"So am I," the farmer replied. "But he has you to thank for it, my boy.
Now all we need is to find him a good, safe home where he'll be lightly worked and highly valued."
For a couple of months, the pair took me out with the carriage fairly often.
Soon I was back in shape and pulling them happily all around the neighborhood.
One day the grooms spent extra time getting me ready.
They made my black coat shine, trimmed the stray hairs off my legs, and polished my hooves.
Even the harness seemed extra clean.
When Willie arrived, he seemed happy and anxious at the same time.
"Do you think they'll like him, Grandpa?" he asked the farmer.
"I don't know, my boy. All we can do is give it a try."
They got into the carriage and picked up the reins.
We headed out of the farm and down the road.
I wasn't sure where we were going, but I knew that something unusual was about to happen.
A few miles down the road, Willie and his grandfather brought me to a halt in front of a pretty cottage.
The farmer went to the door while Willie stayed with me.
Three ladies came out of the house.
One was tall and pale and wrapped in a shawl.
She was leaning on the arm of a younger lady with dark eyes and a cheerful face.
The third lady was tall with a kind smile.
They all came over to see me.
The cheerful younger lady, whose name was Miss Ellen, seemed to take to me right away.
"He has a good face," she said, giving me a pat. "I like him already!"
The tall, pale lady, Miss Lavinia, glanced at my knees.
"I don't know," she said.
"I'd always be nervous riding behind a horse that's fallen down before."
"Many fine horses have scars on their knees, thanks to careless drivers," the farmer said.
"I suspect that's what happened to this horse.
But I don't blame you for being cautious.
If you like, you can take him on trial for a while and see what your coachman thinks of him."
The tall lady, Miss Blomefield, nodded.
"You've never steered us wrong on a horse yet," she told the farmer.
"If my sisters agree, we'll gladly give him a try."
The next day a handsome young man arrived to pick me up.
At first he looked pleased. Then he saw my knees and his expression changed.
"I didn't think you'd recommend a blemished horse to the ladies, sir," he told the farmer.
"I know you're a good judge of horses, young man," the farmer replied.
"Just give him a fair trial.
I think you'll see that he's the safest horse you could want for your ladies."
The young man agreed and led me back to the ladies' home.
I was put into a comfortable stall. The young man fed me and left me to rest.
The next day, after I'd finished my breakfast, he took me out of my stall and started to groom me.
He pushed aside my forelock to brush my face, and then stopped.
"That looks just like the star Black Beauty had," he murmured.
"This horse is about the same height too. I wonder where old Beauty is now."
He continued with his grooming.
Soon he came to the little knot I'd had in my neck for years.
The groom looked startled.
He began to look me over carefully, talking to himself all the while.
"White star, one white foot, this little knot just in that spot . . .
I can't believe it, here's the little patch of white hair on his back too!
Oh Beauty, it is you! Black Beauty, do you remember me?
It's Joe, Little Joe Green!"
He began patting me all over, laughing with delight.
I can't say I would have recognized him, all grown up as he was.
I put my nose up to him to show him that I knew we were friends.
"Give you a fair trial!" Little Joe exclaimed with a laugh.
"I should think so! I wonder who ruined your knees, my old Beauty.
You must have had some hard times somewhere along the way.
But you'll have only the best from now on if I have anything to do with it!
I only wish John Manly were here to see you."
That afternoon Little Joe harnessed me and brought me to the house.
Miss Ellen came out to try me, with Little Joe riding along.
She was a good driver and seemed pleased with my paces.
Little Joe told her that he was sure I was Squire Gordon's old Black Beauty.
When we returned, Miss Ellen told her sisters all about it.
"I'll write to Mrs. Gordon right away and let her know her favorite horse has come to us," she said.
"She'll be so happy to hear it!"
The sisters drove me every day for the next week.
Even Miss Lavinia finally found the courage to ride along with the others.
They decided to keep me and call me by my old name of Black Beauty.
That was a year ago, and I'm still with them and as happy as I've ever been.
Little Joe and the ladies treat me kindly.
My work is easy and pleasant, and my strength and spirits are back.
Willie and his grandfather come to visit often, and the ladies have promised never to sell me.
And so this is where my story ends. My troubles are all over, and I am at home.
Often, before I am quite awake, I imagine that I am still in the orchard at Birtwick Park, standing with my old friends under the apple trees.
